5. A first recipe

David Sarrat González

Source: vignettes/book-05-recipe.Rmd
book-05-recipe.Rmd

What you will learn

Build education and cause-of-death columns, predict its output, and request category counts.

This chapter uses the synthetic questionnaire dataset described in Getting started. You need: the packages and the matching practice connection described in Before you start. Run the sections in order in one R session. All printed results below were computed with dsOMOP and dsOMOPClient 2.10.5. They are teaching data, not clinical findings.

Concept selections refer to the searches and saved definitions in chapter 4, including the separate questionnaire catalogue. Additional body-measurement concepts are found on screen in the formula walkthrough.

Start this chapter

Start a fresh R session in the book-work directory created in Getting started. Run this setup first:

library(dsOMOPClient)
source("tools/book/display.R")
source("tools/book/fixture.R")
practice <- book_fixture()
conns <- practice$conns
names(conns)
#> [1] "site"

The site connection is ready. This chapter creates its temporary questionnaire fixture locally.

Select the education question

An event describes records of interest. It is a definition on your computer, not a downloaded table. We have switched from chapter 4’s GiBleed asthma search to the questionnaire fixture. First look up its education question by concept:

question <- ds.omop.concept.lookup(900001L, conns = conns)
knitr::kable(question$pooled["concept_name"])
concept_name
Education question

Now use that question to select observations:

education_event <- omop_event("observation", concepts = 900001L)
class(education_event)
#> [1] "omop_event" "list"

The server will select observations whose question is Education question.

Choose one answer per person

A reducer turns possibly many records into one value. Use the latest nonmissing coded answer, ordered by the observation date:

education <- omop_variable(
  event = education_event,
  reducer = omop_reduce("last_value", value = "value_as_concept_id"))
class(education)
#> [1] "omop_variable" "list"

This makes one categorical column. It does not create a separate binary column for every education level. A same-date tie uses the documented deterministic record ordering; it does not mean “largest answer ID”.

Add cause of death 

cause <- omop_variable(
  event = omop_event("death"),
  reducer = omop_reduce("first_value", value = "cause_concept_id"))
class(cause)
#> [1] "omop_variable" "list"

Here the value comes from cause_concept_id. Do not substitute cause_source_value: that is free source text, not the curated coded cause used by this route.

Describe a wide table

Wide means one column per variable. Person grain means one row per person. The native all-person population retains people who have neither answer nor death.

people <- omop_recipe(
  variables = list(education = education, cause_of_death = cause),
  outputs = omop_output("people", format = "wide", grain = "person"))
class(people)
#> [1] "omop_recipe" "list"

person_id is included automatically as a pseudonym. Missing records produce missing values. The roster does not require an extra identifier variable.

Predict: read the recipe explanation 

explained <- recipe_explain(people, conns = conns)
cat(explained$text, sep = "\n")
#> Recipe plan
#> Population 'base' (criteria): none
#> Variables:
#>   education: last_value of event 'obs_900001' (value 'value_as_concept_id') over any time; missing = "skip"
#>   cause_of_death: first_value of event 'death' (value 'cause_concept_id') over any time; missing = "skip"
#> Output 'people' [wide] rows 'base', grain person
#> Published: people
#> Defaults relied on:
#>   - variable 'education': rows with a NULL value are skipped before the row is selected (missing = "skip")
#>   - variable 'cause_of_death': rows with a NULL value are skipped before the row is selected (missing = "skip")
#> Concept presentation: factors; identity is the declared concept class, preserved through aliases and value-preserving reducers.
#> Label precedence: variable recode, recipe recode, vocabulary name, decimal ID fallback. Explicit equal recodes merge categories.
#> Federation: permitted ID union, including declared unused levels; newest comparable vocabulary version, then bytewise name tie. Unresolved versions never establish recency.
#> Generated names: ASCII snake_case vocabulary tokens; colliding automatic names gain concept-ID suffixes. Vocabulary-dependent names are unresolved until permitted federation reconciliation.
#> variables.education: concept origin follows reducer last_value over value_as_concept_id; explicit variable name is retained.
#> variables.cause_of_death: concept origin follows reducer first_value over cause_concept_id; explicit variable name is retained.
#> Execution would use the publication protocol on every site.

Before running, predict one private row per person, two named categorical variables, and a pseudonymous key. With no time restriction, each variable reads all available history independently. That is a teaching definition to choose explicitly in a real study.

Full plan explanation (optional)

A label contract records the category names and their ordering. Federation reconciliation makes those categories agree across sites. A bytewise tie compares the bytes of text to make a repeated choice deterministic. You do not need to configure these for this first recipe.

Read the lines in order: the population defines the row; each variable identifies its source and reducer; output defaults determine the shape; category reconciliation determines names. The explanation contains declarations, not observed patient frequencies.

Print all the chosen defaults:

The explanation above records the chosen defaults before execution.

Run: assign the result 

book_symbols(recipe_execute(people, out = c(people = "D_people"), conns = conns))
#>     people 
#> "D_people"

The reply is a mapping of output names to server symbols. D_people is still on the server. Concept-valued columns are labelled factors because of their declared type. In 2.10.5 the names education and cause_of_death need no _concept_id suffix.

Verify: check what you got

Do this complete check once while learning a new extraction. ds.ls lists server symbols; ds.dim describes the result dimensions; ds.colnames names its columns; ds.class checks types. Then inspect one summary or table and missingness with ds.numNA. Every method applies its own release rules. None of these calls retrieves patient rows.

On Opal, ds.ls searches the server workspace. With the installed DSLite/dsBase pair, it searches the R global environment instead, so the filtered result below is deliberately empty. That does not mean extraction failed. The driver’s datashield.symbols method correctly lists the assigned DSLite symbols; we show its D_ analysis objects next. This is a practice-driver difference, not a reason to inspect patient rows.

dsBaseClient::ds.ls(search.filter = "D_*", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> $site$environment.searched
#> [1] "R_GlobalEnv"
#> 
#> $site$objects.found
#> character(0)
#> 
#> $site$search.filter.final
#> [1] "D_*"
lapply(DSI::datashield.symbols(conns), function(x) x[grepl("^D_", x)])
#> $site
#> [1] "D_people"
dsBaseClient::ds.dim("D_people", datasources = conns)
#> $`dimensions of D_people in site`
#> [1] 24  3
#> 
#> $`dimensions of D_people in combined studies`
#> [1] 24  3
dsBaseClient::ds.colnames("D_people", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> [1] "person_id"      "education"      "cause_of_death"
dsBaseClient::ds.class("D_people$education", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> [1] "dsomop_concept_factor" "factor"
dsBaseClient::ds.numNA("D_people$education", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> [1] 12

The category table in the next step completes the check. Compare it with your prediction. Later lessons use at most one helpful schema or variable check per extraction; type checks recur only when the lesson is about types. Explain a recipe again when a new default, censoring, matching or presentation rule matters. This is the predict, run, verify habit of a careful federated analyst.

Count the education categories 

education_table_result <- dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_people$education", useNA = "no", datasources = conns)
knitr::kable(book_counts(education_table_result))
Category Count
Secondary education 6
University education 6

Full aggregate response

education_table_result
#> $output.list
#> $output.list$TABLE_rvar.by.study_row.props
#>                       study
#> D_people$education     site
#>   Secondary education     1
#>   University education    1
#> 
#> $output.list$TABLE_rvar.by.study_col.props
#>                       study
#> D_people$education     site
#>   Secondary education   0.5
#>   University education  0.5
#> 
#> $output.list$TABLE_rvar.by.study_counts
#>                       study
#> D_people$education     site
#>   Secondary education     6
#>   University education    6
#> 
#> $output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_proportions
#> D_people$education
#>  Secondary education University education 
#>                  0.5                  0.5 
#> 
#> $output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts
#> D_people$education
#>  Secondary education University education 
#>                    6                    6 
#> 
#> 
#> $validity.message
#> [1] "Data in all studies were valid"

The Count column answers how many people have each answer. The full response also contains proportions (fractions of a row or column total); we select its TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts component after checking that every site released a valid result. The helper stops on a withheld or incomplete result. The labels are names, not numeric codes. useNA = "no" excludes missing answers; the counts therefore need not add up to the whole population. DataSHIELD checks whether cells may be released before returning the table.

Count causes 

ds.omop.table("D_people", "cause_of_death", conns = conns)
#> D_people$cause_of_death
#> Myocardial infarction             Pneumonia 
#>                    12                     6

ds.omop.table() calls the real dsBase ds.table() and preserves the complete published category contract, including declared zero categories. It also protects labels containing punctuation. Prefer it when you need that complete contract.

Give a question your own yes/no labels 

fever <- omop_variable(
  event = omop_event("observation", concepts = 900002L),
  reducer = omop_reduce("last_value", value = "value_as_concept_id"),
  labels = c("900301" = "yes", "900302" = "no"))
class(fever)
#> [1] "omop_variable" "list"

The map is keyed by answer concepts. It changes presentation, not which question is selected. Missing fever answers remain missing; they do not become “no”.

answers <- omop_recipe(
  variables = list(education = education, fever = fever, cause_of_death = cause),
  outputs = omop_output("people", format = "wide", grain = "person"))
book_symbols(recipe_execute(answers, out = c(people = "D_answers"), conns = conns))
#>      people 
#> "D_answers"
yes_no_result <- dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_answers$fever", useNA = "no", datasources = conns)
knitr::kable(book_counts(yes_no_result))
Category Count
yes 6
no 6

yes_no_result

#> $output.list$TABLE_rvar.by.study_row.props

#> D_answers$fever site

#>             no     1
#> 
#> $output.list$TABLE_rvar.by.study_col.props

#> D_answers$fever site
#>             yes  0.5
#>             no   0.5
#> 
#> $output.list$TABLE_rvar.by.study_counts
#>                study
#> D_answers$fever site

#>             no     6

The table contains your lower-case labels. See chapter 10 for the same operation across two different vocabularies.

Try it

Count education using the complete-contract helper instead of calling ds.table directly.

Solution

ds.omop.table("D_people", "education", conns = conns)
#> D_people$education
#>  Secondary education University education 
#>                    6                    6

Exercise 2: a common variant

Count causes with dsBase directly, preserving missing causes.

Solution 2

knitr::kable(book_counts(dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_people$cause_of_death", useNA = "always", datasources = conns)))
Category Count
Myocardial infarction 12
Pneumonia 6
NA 6

Missing cause is not another coded cause and not proof that a person survived.

Exercise 3: a pitfall to avoid

Verify the combined answer table has the three intended variables.

Solution 3

dsBaseClient::ds.colnames("D_answers", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> [1] "person_id"      "education"      "fever"          "cause_of_death"

The pseudonymous person key is automatic. The education, fever and cause columns come from separate declarations.

Recap

An event selects records, a reducer selects a value, and a wide output arranges private rows. Only the aggregate returns to you.
